adapts the packet to the MTU below

Different link technologies have different carrying capacity. Each has its own MTU (Maximum Transfer Unit): the maximum size it can carry.

If the transport layer delivers a 20,000-byte packet and the data link layer has Ethernet, the capacity is much smaller. IP must adapt the packet to the limitations of the link protocol.

That IP mechanism is fragmentation and reassembly.
The MTU is imposed by the network below; it is IP that adapts.
A single datagram may have to cross networks with very different MTUs before reaching its destination.
From A to B, with a smaller network in the middle

A wants to send a message to B. It sends R1 an IP datagram with a total length of 1500 bytes, the maximum its network allows.

R1 examines the destination IP and decides it has to send it out the NET 2 interface. But that interface has an MTU of 620 bytes: the datagram does not fit in the network it must cross.
The problem shows up midway: A does not know which networks lie ahead.
R1 looks at the destination IP → it must exit via NET 2 → that interface's MTU is 620 and the datagram is 1500.

R1 splits the datagram into fragments that do fit in the 620 MTU and sends them out that interface.

When an IP datagram is fragmented, it becomes multiple IP datagrams: each fragment carries its own header.

Of the 1500 bytes, 20 are header and 1480 are data. The data is divided into 600 + 600 + 280 and each part gets a 20-byte header.
One datagram goes into R1; three come out.

R2 receives three datagrams. It does not know they are fragments: it switches them as if they were three different datagrams destined for B.

At B, the IP protocol receives three datagrams whose headers say they are fragments of a larger packet. IP takes them, rebuilds the original datagram and delivers it to the transport layer.

IP is what fragments and what reassembles.
The router that needs to fragments; only the destination reassembles.
R2 does not join them back, even if the next network has an MTU of 1500: to it they are three datagrams like any other. Only B recovers the 1500 bytes.

Each fragment becomes an independent datagram, with its own header.

The three headers share immutable data, copied from the original:

  • the identifier,
  • the source IP,
  • the destination IP.

That way the destination knows all three belong to the same datagram. What changes from one to the next are a flag and the offset field, which say what place that piece occupies.
Same identifier and same addresses = fragments of the same datagram.
Above, the original: 20 + 600 + 600 + 280 = 1500 bytes. Below, what travels over NET 2: 620 + 620 + 300 = 1540 bytes. Each fragment pays for its own header.
The offset and the "more fragments" flag

The offset indicates where the fragment's data goes within the original: at byte 0, 600 and 1200.

But the absolute value is not stored: it would take a field as large as the length. To shrink it, it is written in multiples of 8 bytes: 600 is 75 blocks and 1200 is 150.

The more fragments flag is 0 if it is the last (or only) fragment. With it, the destination checks whether it already has them all.
Offset = position in bytes ÷ 8. More fragments = 0 only in the last one.
600 ÷ 8 = 75 · 1200 ÷ 8 = 150. The Offset field has 13 bits; counting in units of 8 bytes is enough to place a piece anywhere in a datagram of up to 65,535 bytes.

The other flag, don't fragment, prevents fragmentation.

If a router needs to fragment a datagram and that bit is set, it cannot: it discards the packet.

Another protocol also runs on routers, ICMP, which steps in in this case: it is used to tell the source that the datagram could not continue.
With "don't fragment", if it doesn't fit whole, it doesn't get through.
DF = 1: the 1500-byte datagram has the don't fragment bit set. R1 cannot split it: it discards it and the notice goes back toward A.

Fragmenting turns one datagram into several, and IP is unreliable: each one has its own probability of being lost. If we split a datagram into three, the probability of loss triples.

It also creates more processing load on routers, which must fragment and create a packet for each fragment.

That is why an application can request don't fragment. Nowadays, most do.
Three fragments = three chances to lose the whole datagram.
Just one fragment was lost, but B cannot rebuild the datagram: the other two traveled for nothing.

Fragmentation can be done repeatedly. If further on there is an interface with an even smaller MTU, the fragments must be fragmented.

Since fragments already come with an offset, the new offset is calculated relative to the original datagram, not to the fragment being split.

In the example, R3 must send the three fragments out a network with MTU 576: instead of three, five arrive, each with its place in the original.
No matter how many times it is split: the offset always refers to the original datagram.

MTU 576 − 20 header = 556. Since the offset counts in units of 8 bytes, each piece that is not the last carries a multiple of 8: 552.
F1b keeps more fragments = 1: F2 and F3 still come after it.

• Each network has its MTU; if the datagram doesn't fit, the router fragments it.
  • Each fragment is an independent datagram; only the destination reassembles.
  • They share the identification, source IP and destination IP.
  • Offset in units of 8 bytes (0, 75, 150) and the more fragments flag (0 in the last one).
  • Don't fragment: if it doesn't fit, it is discarded. Fragmenting multiplies the probability of loss and loads the routers.

We now know what a datagram carries. What remains is how to identify who it is addressed to: in the next lesson, IP addressing.

The first router whose network has a large enough MTU
No one: the transport layer receives the three separately
Intermediate routers switch the fragments as independent datagrams; only IP at the destination rebuilds the original.
A fragment carries data that starts at byte 1200 of the original datagram. What value does its offset field have?
The offset is written in multiples of 8 bytes: 1200 ÷ 8 = 150.
In which fragment is the "more fragments" flag 0?
In the last (or in an unfragmented datagram)
It is 0 if it is the last or only fragment; that way the destination knows where the datagram ends and can check whether it has them all.

It is trimmed to the MTU size
It stays queued until the MTU changes
